title: Data Security and Governance
objective: Explain how to combine access control, encryption, masking, auditing, and governance based on data classification, owners, users, operations, and audit requirements.

sections.title: Separating Who Accesses What and for What Purpose
paragraphs: When designing data access, do not stop at broad groups such as “analysts.” Define separately the identity of the person or workload, the required datasets, the permitted operations, the environment in which they will be used, and the time limit. Authentication verifies the person or workload, while authorization determines which operations that principal is permitted to perform.

AWS Lake Formation manages fine-grained access control for data in data lakes on Amazon S3 and the related metadata in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Instead of broadly granting IAM permissions so that “analysts can read everything,” design the scope—such as tables, columns, and rows—according to data classification and business need.

An application’s execution role and a role assumed by a person for analysis are separate principals. Do not provide access through shared, fixed credentials. Giving each principal only the permissions and audit records it needs reduces unnecessary access and enables later tracing.

sources.label: DEA-C01 Domain 4: Data Security and Governance

sections.title: Decide How to Present and Protect Data Based on Its Sensitivity
paragraphs: To protect data, first classify what constitutes sensitive information. Names, contact details, account information, identifiers, and similar data can differ in nature and purpose of use for each dataset or column. Do not decide based solely on the phrase “encrypted.” Instead, distinguish who needs plaintext, what should be hidden when displayed, and whether to protect the data at rest, in transit, or in backups.

Encryption is an important way to prevent unauthorized entities from reading data at rest or in transit. However, to avoid showing unnecessary personal information to analysts who legitimately have read permissions, combine authorization for columns or rows with masking, summarized data, and similar measures.

Changing keys, access permissions, or masking rules can cause existing users or pipelines to fail. Before making changes, verify the affected data, users, and recovery procedures, and test both access denial and excessive exposure.

sections.title: Clarifying the Responsibilities of Owners, Stewards, and Users
paragraphs: Data governance determines not only where data is stored, but also who is responsible for its meaning and quality. Data owners are responsible for the business purpose and definition of a dataset, whether it may be used, and approval of changes. Data engineers implement and operate the agreed mechanisms for ingestion, transformation, storage, and access.

AWS Glue Data Catalog centrally manages locations, schemas, and properties, providing a foundation for finding and understanding datasets. By associating business terms, quality requirements, classifications, owners, and update frequencies with the catalog, users can judge not only whether they can read the data, but also what it means and how far it can be trusted.

When data has no known owner, there is no designated person or team to decide how to handle quality anomalies, schema changes, deletion requests, or access requests. Before publishing a new dataset, record its owner, steward, users, approval path, and contact point.

sections.title: Audits Must Preserve Access Facts and the Grounds for Decisions
paragraphs: Audits require more than the configurations that permitted access. You must be able to trace when access occurred, which principal accessed which data, what operation was performed, and which approvals and rules supported the decision. Because data-content change history and AWS API operation history serve different purposes, retain both types of evidence and link them together.

AWS CloudTrail can be used to track AWS API calls. Operators determine how long logs must be retained for investigating anomalous access, how log integrity will be maintained, who may view them, and where they will be stored. Granting broad access to audit logs can instead expose confidential and operational information unnecessarily.

During regular permission reviews, do not make decisions based only on current job titles. Verify the datasets and operations actually required, the expiration dates, and usage history. Remove permissions that are no longer needed, and record the expiration date and approver for exceptions.

checkpoints.prompt: HR analysts want to view only the columns needed to aggregate employee data by department. They do not need to view salary amounts or personal contact information. Which method is most appropriate for the data administrator to implement least privilege?

choices.text: Grant all analysts permission to read every file in the data lake.
choices.explanation: They could view salary amounts and contact information that are not needed for their work, so this would not implement least privilege.

choices.text: Allow the analysts’ role to access only the necessary datasets and columns, and exclude the other columns from the access scope.
choices.explanation: Correct. Separating the principal, resource, and operation and authorizing only the necessary scope implements least privilege appropriate to the intended use.

choices.text: If salary amounts are encrypted, it is acceptable to give all analysts permission to decrypt them as well.
choices.explanation: Encryption is important, but allowing users who do not need the data to decrypt and view it does not prevent excessive exposure.

choices.text: Have the HR department and the analysts share and reuse a common access key.
choices.explanation: With shared credentials, the principals cannot be distinguished, so activity cannot be tracked and permissions cannot be minimized.

checkpoints.prompt: The data owner of a payment service is adding a new personally identifiable information column to a transaction dataset. The data engineer wants to avoid exposing it to unnecessary users without stopping existing aggregation processes. Which change procedure is most appropriate?

choices.text: Immediately after adding the column, automatically grant all existing roles permission to view it.
choices.explanation: Users who do not need the personally identifiable information would be able to view it, which contradicts data classification and least-privilege principles.

choices.text: Because it contains personally identifiable information, delete the entire dataset and stop the aggregation.
choices.explanation: Deleting and stopping everything without designing the necessary protections would unnecessarily harm the intended use and availability.

choices.text: Classify the column, confirm the affected processes and users, and then configure visibility and access scope only for the roles that need it.
choices.explanation: Correct. The schema change can be managed together with its classification, intended use, permissions, and impact on existing processes.

choices.text: Change only the data format without recording the meaning and owner of the new column.
choices.explanation: Without knowing the meaning, owner, and conditions of use, it is impossible to make appropriate access-approval or data-quality decisions.

checkpoints.prompt: A financial company’s auditor wants to determine later why an analytics job accessed customer data. The data administrator must retain both evidence that the access occurred and the basis for the authorization decision. Which combination of records is most appropriate?

choices.text: Save only a screen capture of the current permissions settings and retain no record of the operations performed at runtime.
choices.explanation: The current settings alone cannot show when, by whom, or which operations were performed.

choices.text: Do not create audit logs because they might contain sensitive information.
choices.explanation: Viewing permissions should be appropriately restricted; this is not a reason to omit the necessary audit trail.

choices.text: Record only the data owner’s name and do not record the accessing principal or the operations performed.
choices.explanation: The owner identifies who is responsible for the decision, but this does not replace records showing the actual accessing principal, target, and operations.

choices.text: Correlate the job execution record, the target dataset, the assumed role, the basis for the approval and classification, and records of AWS API operations.
choices.explanation: Correct. This makes it possible to verify both the fact of the execution and why that principal was authorized to access that scope, which supports auditing and investigation.
